title: When no single pattern fits a part
idea: MEET: if a sub-problem seems to need two patterns at once, that's a sign it should be split further into smaller parts.

exercises.prompt: A sub-problem is 'the average of the big orders'. It seems to need filter AND total AND divide. What does that tell you?
options: Split it further into smaller single-pattern parts
Pick just one pattern and ignore the rest
Give up
Use no pattern
exercises.explanation: Needing several patterns means the part is still too big. Split it into filter, then total/count, then divide.

exercises.prompt: If one sub-problem needs several patterns, it should be split into smaller sub-problems.
exercises.explanation: Yes — one part, one pattern. Needing several is the signal to decompose that part further.

exercises.prompt: 'The average of the passing scores' is best seen as...
options: several small parts, each with one pattern
one part with no pattern
one giant pattern
impossible
exercises.explanation: It's filter + total + count + divide — four small single-pattern parts, not one blurry step.

exercises.prompt: Select the sub-problems that are still too big (need splitting further).
options: the average of the orders over 100
the total AND the count in one breath
total the prices
count the passers
exercises.explanation: The first two bundle multiple jobs. The last two are each a single clean pattern.

exercises.prompt: Why aim for 'one part, one pattern'?
options: Each part becomes a known loop shape you can code directly
To make more parts for fun
Patterns dislike company
It's a rule with no reason
exercises.explanation: A single-pattern part maps straight to code. Bundled parts hide the shape and invite bugs.

exercises.prompt: A part that needs two patterns is fine to leave as-is.
exercises.explanation: No — leave it and you'll write tangled code. Split it so each piece has one clear pattern.

exercises.prompt: Match each 'too big' part to how it splits.
exercises.explanation: Each bundled part breaks into single-pattern pieces. Splitting further is just more decomposition.

exercises.prompt: How deep do you keep splitting?
options: Until every part is a single familiar pattern
Until there are exactly two parts
Forever
Never — one part is always enough
exercises.explanation: Stop when each part is one pattern you know. That's the natural floor for decomposition.

blocks: Try to label a part with one pattern
If it needs several, split the part into smaller parts
Label each smaller part with its single pattern
exercises.explanation: Attempt a label; if it resists, split again; then label the pieces. Recursion by hand, no code.

options: If a part needs several patterns, split it further until each part has exactly one
Big parts are fine
Never split a part twice
One pattern can do everything
exercises.explanation: One part, one pattern. When a part resists a single label, decompose it further.
